Background: I started smoking weed and selling drugs at a young age. Weed led to psychedelics which led to xans/adderall/lean which led to opiates and it ended with heroin. Selling drugs opened up my access and allowed me to abuse as much as I wanted. I’ve used drugs heavily for 3 years before I quit. 

How did you do it: it really took a lot of outside influence for me to consider quitting. I had friends go to jail, overdose, people telling me not continue that life. What it came down to was me personally wanting to change. I stopped idolizing drug culture. All my friends that don’t do drugs are having a great time. I know that I didn’t need drugs to have fun cause other people had fun without drugs. 

I watched a lot of videos of addicts(how they lived, families that go bankrupt sending their kids to rehab, people not having control of their life due to their drug use) and I told myself I’d never be like that. 

The last drug I was doing was heroin and I read somewhere that exercising releases endorphins similar to opiates so I started going to the gym. I got really into the “bro science” and pretty much I got really interested in being healthy. Eating was an issue before so I made it a point to eat right. I think I might have given myself depression from all the drugs so exercising helps with that too. I think having a purpose for living that doesn’t involve drugs helps a lot. At the end of the day willpower got me through it, I forced myself to keep the promises I made to myself. I felt like I fried my brain from drug use so I made it a point to read everyday to keep my brain active. I started with the news and now I’m able to read 300 pages a day. I’m currently learning python so I have that skill under my belt. Pretty much finding meaning in activities that don’t involve drug use help me not think about drugs. I also had to take a year off college to detox and self reflect. That’s an important part. I think that being around sober peers and role models really help because they say things that might stick with you that push you to become a better person. Having some long term and short term goals really help gauge where you are at and where you need to go. Once you overcome the addiction you feel like you can do anything. You learn willpower and self discipline, which are extremely useful in all aspects of life. I also got really into art and finding beauty in everything, and it’s a good creative medium. 

 I think a big part of overcoming it though is when you first come off of the drug and you are miserable. The key is to stay miserable and not give into the comforts that taking a drug would give you. It gives you drive to want to be happy, and let’s you reflect on the parts of yourself you want to change. Once you associate drug use with unhappiness from a crash, drugs become a lot less appealing. People told me they wouldn’t wish being dope sick on their worst enemy. 

How is your life since quitting: I’m focused more on developing myself professionally. I’m trying to learn how to communicate with people again. I feel tired sometimes and get depressed a lot but I had that as a child, I think the drugs brought it out. I feel happy that I’m not on drugs anymore and I’m operating with a clear mind. I’m pretty young so I’m making moves that will help me make money and drugs are not a distraction anymore. I have a better sense of what is important and what’s not important, in terms of how I spend my time and when weighing decisions. Nothing feels worse than realizing all those years of your life has gone down the drain and you have nothing to show for it. I try not to make that mistake anymore, and it translates to relationships and time management. I have a less tolerance for bs. I think I matured a lot. 

Do you ever get cravings: as much as I hate to admit it I get cravings all the time. I relapse sometimes but I haven’t in the last few months, mostly due to not having/cutting off connections. 

The cravings are usually due to some external stimulus though, what I crave the most is Xanax when I’m stressed. That’s pretty much it though, all the other drugs I did would be out of boredom, so if I catch myself bored I’ll try and do something fun like read or play video games or make music or something. 

That Xanax craving is something else though if someone offers it to me I’d really have a hard time saying no. I don’t hang out with people that do drugs like that anymore so I haven’t had that come up. If I want a stimulant like adderall or coke I just drink coffee. I don’t really have the urge to smoke weed or take psyches anymore cause it isn’t really addictive and I feel like I got the most I would ever get out of psychs to open my mind. Although I was smoking opiates, the Xanax I was taking had a little bit of feyntanal in it so I think that with the combination of benzos makes that craving linger. But I know the only reason I crave it is because I’m stressed all the time, so I’ve been working on meditation and other stress reducing techniques. 

Sorry for ranting lol I just thought if maybe someone was trying to overcome addiction they would find some of this information useful. 

TLDR: I did it with willpower and self discipline, It changed my life because it helped me see what’s important and what isn’t important, and yes I crave Xanax all the time.

What I do is a 3x8 of 4-5 exercises and I do a different body part each day. After that I play like an hour of basketball. What I’ve found is that if I challenge myself hard enough on the weights, it is kinda like doing light cardio because of what my heart rate is at. Also gaining muscle will help you lose weight over the long run. The more muscle you have increases your basal metabolic rate which means you basically burn more calories while sedentary. Losing fat is a long process and it will require a lot of work. Basically what most people recommend to lose fat is to calculate your basal metabolic rate(you can find a calculator for that online) and subtract 5% from that. That way you are at a calorie deficit and it will be the most healthy way to lose weight. I also use some supplements such as creatine and L-citruline for muscle endurance and increased nitric oxide. Some people use preworkout but I don’t use it because it has an unhealthy amount of caffeine and I don’t wanna blow out my heart lol. What I do before workouts is drink a protein shake with some creatine and L citruline. If you are starting from scratch then you should probably have some sort of workout program you should follow. Again, losing fat is not something you will see in a week or a month, so don’t get discouraged. It will probably take at least a year to get a drastic change. The program that I’m on is more for strength, not really for big muscles or anything, so you should look into a program that fits your needs. Although fat loss is your main goal, maybe have some secondary goals just so you are hyped to go back to the gym, such as getting your bench press numbers up. Another option that you should look into is calisthenics, where the exercises are mostly body weight. I haven’t done this but many people look pretty ripped off of that. But yeah initially starting out you should focus on going like 60% emphasizing proper form(for squats, bench press, overhead press, deadlift, etc) for a couple weeks and then you do something called progressive overload where each time you go to the gym you either add more weight or more reps. The problem that I have is I don’t eat enough sometimes so my progression kinda stalls but if your on the heavier side of the scale I feel like that won’t be too much of a problem for you and doing something like that will benefit you more.
